title: The rows a gas utility's project appears in

blocks.text: A gas utility (a fictional one) plans its fleets (mains, valves, regulators) with the same multi-period model as GridCap: a binary $`x_{i,t}`$ for every project $`i`$ and every start year $`t`$ from its earliest to its latest. When a test of the model fails, the first question is "which rows does this project's variables appear in?". Write the function that answers it.
The model's rows, with the names the code gives them:

items: `must_<id>` if the project is a must-do, otherwise `once_<id>`: the sum of its start variables.
`alt_<group>` for a project in an alternative group.

`after_<child>_<t>` for each child project and each of the child's start years $`t`$: $`\text{by}(\text{child}, t) \le \text{by}(\text{parent}, t - \text{lag})`$, where $`\text{by}(i, t)`$ is the sum of project $`i`$'s start variables for years up to $`t`$. A variable appears in a row only if the row has a term for it.
`budget_<y>` for each plan year $`y`$, summing the spend of every project at work in $`y`$; a project started in $`t`$ with a duration of $`d`$ years is at work in years $`t`$ to $`t + d - 1`$.
`crew_<program>_<y>`, the same as the budget row but one per program.

blocks.text: Write `rows_for(pid, projects, years)` in `rows.py`: the set of row names in which at least one of project `pid`'s start variables appears. Only years in `years` have budget and crew rows.

A parent's variable is in a child's `after_<child>_<t>` row only when the row's right-hand side can reach it: $`\text{by}(\text{parent}, t - \text{lag})`$ sums the parent's starts up to $`t - \text{lag}`$, so the parent appears exactly when $`t - \text{lag}`$ is at least the parent's earliest start. Worked example: a parent P that may start only in 2028, and its child C (start 2028 to 2030, lag 1).

items: `after_C_2028`: the right side is $`\text{by}(P, 2027)`$, which sums no variable of P (P cannot start by 2027), so P is not in this row.
`after_C_2029`: the right side is $`\text{by}(P, 2028) = x_{P,2028}`$, so P is in it.
`after_C_2030`: the right side is $`\text{by}(P, 2029) = x_{P,2028}`$, so P is in it.

blocks.text: So P's rows are `once_P`, `after_C_2029`, `after_C_2030` and its budget and crew rows for 2028; C's own variables are in all three of C's after rows. The tests use small hand-made fleets. About fifteen lines.

"""Run executes this file. Change the calls and see what prints. Submit grades."""
import logging

# Turn the logger up, so the `log.debug` lines of your code show under the printed lines.
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG, format="%(levelname)s %(message)s")

from rows import Project, rows_for

years = [2030, 2031, 2032, 2033]
projects = [Project("T1", "transformers", 2030, 2031, 2),
            Project("T2", "transformers", 2032, 2033, 1, parent="T1", lag=1),
            Project("B1", "breakers", 2031, 2031, 1, must_do=True),
            Project("C1", "cables", 2033, 2033, 1, alt_group="K"),
            Project("C2", "cables", 2033, 2033, 1, alt_group="K")]

for pid in ("T1", "T2", "B1", "C2"):
    print(f"rows of {pid}:", sorted(rows_for(pid, projects, years)))

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Project:
    pid: str
    program: str
    earliest: int
    latest: int
    duration: int                  # years of work
    must_do: bool = False
    alt_group: str | None = None
    parent: str | None = None
    lag: int = 0


def rows_for(pid: str, projects: list[Project], years: list[int]) -> set[str]:
    """The names of every row in which one of project `pid`'s start variables appears."""
    # TODO: go through the model's rows one kind at a time. The empty set is a placeholder.
    return set()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    projects = [Project("S1", "substations", 2027, 2028, 2), Project("S2", "substations", 2029, 2029, 1, parent="S1", lag=1)]
    print(sorted(rows_for("S1", projects, [2027, 2028, 2029])))

cases.says: a project with one start year is in its once row and the budget and crew rows of its years of work
a must-do is in its must row, and an option is in its group's row
a parent's variables appear in its children's precedence rows, not only the child's
a parent is in a child's row only for child years its own start years can precede
the budget and crew rows cover every allowed start, not only the earliest

origin.section: Each Fleet Brings Its Own Rows to the Model

concepts: each project's attributes decide which once, must, alternative, precedence, budget and crew rows it appears in
